claim: rTMS over the aPFC applied before threat memory retrieval immediately decreases implicit reactions to learned stimuli in humans
source: Here we showed that rTMS over the aPFC applied before threat memory retrieval immediately decreases implicit reactions to learned and novel stimuli in humans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced SCRs in the aPFC group compared to sham during the test session (Figure 2B-E)

claim: rTMS over the aPFC applied before threat memory retrieval immediately decreases implicit reactions to novel stimuli in humans
source: Here we showed that rTMS over the aPFC applied before threat memory retrieval immediately decreases implicit reactions to learned and novel stimuli in humans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing overall attenuated responses to tones (NS1, CS, NS2) in the aPFC group relative to sham (Figure 2D-E)

claim: The effects of rTMS over the aPFC on implicit reactions enduringly persisted 1 week later in the absence of rTMS
source: These effects enduringly persisted 1 week later in the absence of rTMS.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that the aPFC group persisted in displaying weaker SCRs than the sham group during the follow-up session (Figure 2G-H)

claim: rTMS over the aPFC had no effects on explicit recognition
source: No effects were detected on explicit recognition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in explicit recognition accuracy between aPFC-E and sham-E groups (Figure 3A, C)

claim: rTMS over the aPFC resulted in a more pronounced reduction of defensive responses compared to rTMS targeting the dorsolateral PFC
source: Critically, rTMS over the aPFC resulted in a more pronounced reduction of defensive responses compared to rTMS targeting the dorsolateral PFC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing weaker defensive responses in the aPFC group relative to the dlPFC group during test and follow-up sessions (Figure 5B-C, G-H)

claim: Emotional memories related to past threat experiences allow humans to predict future dangers and trigger adaptive defensive reactions when encountering learned threat-signaling cues
source: Emotional memories related to past threat experiences allow humans to predict future dangers and trigger adaptive defensive reactions when encountering learned threat-signaling cues (DiFazio et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to DiFazio et al., 2022

claim: Extremely dangerous situations may lead to psychological disorders
source: However, extremely dangerous situations may lead to psychological disorders (Wilker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilker et al., 2014

claim: Evaluation mechanisms excessively biased toward threat generalization may underlie anxiety disorders and trauma
source: On the other hand, evaluation mechanisms excessively biased toward threat generalization (i.e. overgeneralization) may underlie anxiety disorders and trauma (Dunsmoor and Paz, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dunsmoor and Paz, 2015

claim: Autonomic-implicit and cognitive-explicit tunings may diverge when humans are exposed to the same new stimuli
source: At the base of these processes, in a previous work (Manassero et al., 2019). we observed that autonomic-implicit and cognitive-explicit tunings may diverge when humans are exposed to the same new stimuli, where cognitive generalization may enable a flexible evaluation of incoming cues to develop adaptive predictions of potential dangers.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Manassero et al., 2019

claim: Common approaches such as pharmacological treatments and cognitive-behavioral therapy have demonstrated partial efficacy for anxiety and post-traumatic disorders
source: Common approaches such as pharmacological treatments and cognitive-behavioral therapy have demonstrated partial efficacy (Taylor et al., 2012), and recent evidence suggests that the functional outcome of behavioral methods may depend on the extent to which the prefrontal cortex is recruited during these processes (Fonzo et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taylor et al., 2012 and Fonzo et al., 2017a

claim: The functional outcome of behavioral methods may depend on the extent to which the prefrontal cortex is recruited during these processes
source: Common approaches such as pharmacological treatments and cognitive-behavioral therapy have demonstrated partial efficacy (Taylor et al., 2012), and recent evidence suggests that the functional outcome of behavioral methods may depend on the extent to which the prefrontal cortex is recruited during these processes (Fonzo et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fonzo et al., 2017a

claim: Previous studies adopted transcranial direct current stimulation or transcranial electrical stimulation to disrupt the consolidation of threat memories
source: Previous studies adopted transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) or transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) to disrupt the consolidation of these memories (Asthana et al., 2013; Mungee et al., 2014; Mungee et al., 2016), potentiate extinction processes (Abend et al., 2016; van 't Wout et al., 2016), and narrow threat generalization patterns (Roesmann et al., 2022), leading to contradictory results.
evidence: Supported by citations to Asthana et al., 2013; Mungee et al., 2014; Mungee et al., 2016

claim: Cathodal stimulation over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex disrupted threat memory consolidation, with no enhancing effect of anodal stimulation
source: According to one work (Asthana et al., 2013), cathodal stimulation over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) disrupted threat memory consolidation, with no enhancing effect of anodal stimulation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Asthana et al., 2013

claim: Anodal stimulation over the dlPFC increased implicit responses
source: In contrast, other studies found an increase in implicit responses with anodal stimulation (Mungee et al., 2014) and no effect of cathodal stimulation (Mungee et al., 2016) over the same site.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mungee et al., 2014

claim: Cathodal stimulation over the dlPFC had no effect on implicit responses
source: In contrast, other studies found an increase in implicit responses with anodal stimulation (Mungee et al., 2014) and no effect of cathodal stimulation (Mungee et al., 2016) over the same site.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mungee et al., 2016

claim: Anodal stimulation over the dlPFC revealed an improvement in extinction learning but no delayed effects on the recall of the extinction memory
source: Moreover, one study employing anodal stimulation over the dlPFC (van 't Wout et al., 2016) revealed an improvement in extinction learning but no delayed effects on the recall of the extinction memory.
evidence: Supported by citation to van 't Wout et al., 2016

claim: Low-frequency alternating-current stimulation of the medial prefrontal cortex augmented the defensive responses
source: A further investigation (Abend et al., 2016) reported that low-frequency alternating-current (AC) stimulation of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) augmented the defensive responses, whereas direct-current (DC) stimulation widened threat generalization profiles.
evidence: Supported by citation to Abend et al., 2016

claim: Direct-current stimulation of the medial prefrontal cortex widened threat generalization profiles
source: A further investigation (Abend et al., 2016) reported that low-frequency alternating-current (AC) stimulation of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) augmented the defensive responses, whereas direct-current (DC) stimulation widened threat generalization profiles.
evidence: Supported by citation to Abend et al., 2016

claim: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation ensures greater focality compared to tDCS or tES
source: An alternative neurostimulation approach is repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), which ensures greater focality (Miniussi et al., 2008; Elder and Taylor, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miniussi et al., 2008; Elder and Taylor, 2014

claim: rTMS targeted at the mPFC resulted in successful enhancement of extinction learning
source: Some rTMS studies targeted the mPFC (Guhn et al., 2014) and the posterior PFC (Raij et al., 2018) to obtain a successful enhancement of extinction learning, while others (Borgomaneri et al., 2020; Su et al., 2022) targeted the dlPFC to disrupt threat-memory reconsolidation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Guhn et al., 2014

claim: rTMS targeted at the posterior PFC resulted in successful enhancement of extinction learning
source: Some rTMS studies targeted the mPFC (Guhn et al., 2014) and the posterior PFC (Raij et al., 2018) to obtain a successful enhancement of extinction learning, while others (Borgomaneri et al., 2020; Su et al., 2022) targeted the dlPFC to disrupt threat-memory reconsolidation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Raij et al., 2018

claim: rTMS targeted at the dlPFC was used to disrupt threat-memory reconsolidation
source: Some rTMS studies targeted the mPFC (Guhn et al., 2014) and the posterior PFC (Raij et al., 2018) to obtain a successful enhancement of extinction learning, while others (Borgomaneri et al., 2020; Su et al., 2022) targeted the dlPFC to disrupt threat-memory reconsolidation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Borgomaneri et al., 2020; Su et al., 2022

claim: Fear extinction may be followed by a return of fear with a change of context (renewal)
source: Indeed, most rTMS-based research targeting the PFC has pursued an improvement of fear extinction, which may be followed by a return of fear with a change of context (i.e., renewal) (Vervliet et al., 2013) where prevention of relapse over time is the main challenge for therapies dedicated to post-traumatic and anxiety disorders.
evidence: Supported by citation to Vervliet et al., 2013

claim: No previous studies reported significant effects in downmodulating the defensive responses triggered by a learned threatening stimulus without adopting fear extinction
source: No previous studies reported significant effects in downmodulating the defensive responses triggered by a learned threatening stimulus without adopting fear extinction.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: Human brain stimulation studies have been mainly focused on the dorsolateral region of the PFC
source: So far, human brain stimulation studies have been mainly focused on the dorsolateral region of the PFC (Marković et al., 2021), partly because other prefrontal areas involved in the top-down regulation of subcortical threat-detection systems ‒ such as the ventromedial PFC (vmPFC), are too deep to be reached with TMS (Raij et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marković et al., 2021 and Raij et al., 2018

claim: The ventromedial PFC is too deep to be reached with TMS
source: So far, human brain stimulation studies have been mainly focused on the dorsolateral region of the PFC (Marković et al., 2021), partly because other prefrontal areas involved in the top-down regulation of subcortical threat-detection systems ‒ such as the ventromedial PFC (vmPFC), are too deep to be reached with TMS (Raij et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raij et al., 2018

claim: The anterior prefrontal cortex is a brain structure that is emerging to be engaged in downstream emotional regulation
source: However, within the PFC, a brain structure that is emerging to be engaged in downstream emotional regulation is the anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC), also known as the frontopolar cortex or rostral frontal cortex.
evidence: Based on review of literature and inference from multiple studies

claim: The aPFC encompasses the most anterior portion of the prefrontal cortex (Brodmann area 10)
source: The aPFC encompasses the most anterior portion of the prefrontal cortex (Brodmann area 10 [BA 10]) (Ramnani and Owen, 2004) and extends over a wider cortical space in humans than in other species (Semendeferi et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ramnani and Owen, 2004 and Semendeferi et al., 2001

claim: The aPFC extends over a wider cortical space in humans than in other species
source: The aPFC encompasses the most anterior portion of the prefrontal cortex (Brodmann area 10 [BA 10]) (Ramnani and Owen, 2004) and extends over a wider cortical space in humans than in other species (Semendeferi et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Semendeferi et al., 2001

claim: Many studies highlighted the role of the aPFC in emotional downregulation
source: Even if it has not been included in fear network models so far, many studies (Volman et al., 2013; Koch et al., 2018; Bramson et al., 2020) highlighted its role in emotional downregulation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Volman et al., 2013; Koch et al., 2018; Bramson et al., 2020

claim: Anatomical projections have been found between the lateral aPFC and the amygdala
source: Anatomical projections have been found between the lateral (Bramson et al., 2020; Folloni et al., 2019) and the medial aPFC (Peng et al., 2018) and the amygdala, and functional connectivity has been detected between the aPFC and the vmPFC during fear downregulation (Klumpers et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bramson et al., 2020; Folloni et al., 2019

claim: Anatomical projections have been found between the medial aPFC and the amygdala
source: Anatomical projections have been found between the lateral (Bramson et al., 2020; Folloni et al., 2019) and the medial aPFC (Peng et al., 2018) and the amygdala, and functional connectivity has been detected between the aPFC and the vmPFC during fear downregulation (Klumpers et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peng et al., 2018

claim: Functional connectivity has been detected between the aPFC and the vmPFC during fear downregulation
source: Anatomical projections have been found between the lateral (Bramson et al., 2020; Folloni et al., 2019) and the medial aPFC (Peng et al., 2018) and the amygdala, and functional connectivity has been detected between the aPFC and the vmPFC during fear downregulation (Klumpers et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klumpers et al., 2010

claim: Hypoactivation, reduced connectivity, and altered thickness of aPFC were reported in post-traumatic stress disorder patients
source: Notably, hypoactivation, reduced connectivity, and altered thickness of aPFC were reported in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) patients (Lanius et al., 2005; Morey et al., 2008; Sadeh et al., 2015; Sadeh et al., 2016), whereas a longitudinal study (Kaldewaij et al., 2021) showed that strong activation of the aPFC resulted in a higher resilience against PTSD onset.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lanius et al., 2005; Morey et al., 2008; Sadeh et al., 2015; Sadeh et al., 2016

claim: Strong activation of the aPFC resulted in a higher resilience against PTSD onset
source: Notably, hypoactivation, reduced connectivity, and altered thickness of aPFC were reported in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) patients (Lanius et al., 2005; Morey et al., 2008; Sadeh et al., 2015; Sadeh et al., 2016), whereas a longitudinal study (Kaldewaij et al., 2021) showed that strong activation of the aPFC resulted in a higher resilience against PTSD onset.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaldewaij et al., 2021

claim: Enhanced aPFC activity and potentiated aPFC-vmPFC connectivity were detected after an effective therapy in PTSD patients
source: Accordingly, enhanced aPFC activity and potentiated aPFC-vmPFC connectivity were detected after an effective therapy in PTSD patients (Fonzo et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fonzo et al., 2017b

claim: The aPFC is a surface area easily accessible with rTMS
source: Crucially, the aPFC is a surface area easily accessible with rTMS.
evidence: Based on anatomical knowledge of brain structure and TMS reach

claim: No study has been conducted to explore the effects of aPFC stimulation on the expression of a threat memory without extinction learning in humans
source: However, to our knowledge, no study has been conducted so far to explore the effects of aPFC stimulation on the expression of a threat memory without extinction learning in humans.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: There were no significant differences between groups in post-conditioning US ratings
source: To validate the between-groups homogeneity in the painful stimuli perception, we compared the post-conditioning US ratings and observed no significant differences between groups (Student's unpaired t-test, t(58) = 0.799, p=0.428, ηp2 = 0.011) (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.428)

claim: There were no significant differences between groups in SCRs to the CS during the preconditioning phase
source: We also did not observe significant differences between groups in skin conductance responses (SCRs) to the CS during the preconditioning phase (t(58) = 0.418, p=0.677, ηp2 = 0.003)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.677)

claim: There were no significant differences between groups in SCRs to the CS during the conditioning phase
source: to the CS during the conditioning phase (2 × 15 mixed ANOVA; main effect of group: F(1,52) = 2.367, p=0.130, ηp2 = 0.044; main effect of trial: F(8.762,455.600) = 13.366, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.204; group × trial interaction: F(8.762,455.600) = 1.619, p=0.109, ηp2 = 0.030; Student's unpaired t-test on the averaged response, t(58) = 1.290, p=0.202, ηp2 = 0.028)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (ANOVA, p=0.130 for group effect)

claim: There were no significant differences between groups in SCRs to the US during the conditioning phase
source: nor to the US during the conditioning phase (t(58) = 1.011, p=0.316, ηp2 = 0.017) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.316)

claim: During the test phase, subjects who received rTMS over the aPFC exhibited weakened CS-related SCRs than those observed in the sham group
source: On the contrary, during the test phase subjects who received rTMS over the aPFC exhibited weakened CS-related SCRs than those observed in the sham group (p=0.006; Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.006, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The aPFC group showed reduced autonomic responses to the CS from conditioning to test
source: Moreover, the aPFC group showed reduced autonomic responses to the CS from conditioning to test (p=0.008; Bonferroni corrected)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.008, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The sham group displayed increased mean SCRs to the CS from conditioning to test
source: whereas the sham group displayed increased mean SCRs to the CS from conditioning to test (p=0.018; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.018, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The rTMS procedure affected SCRs triggered by memory retrieval performed shortly after rTMS
source: This data indicates that the rTMS procedure affected SCRs triggered by memory retrieval performed shortly after rTMS.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing differential effects between aPFC and sham groups

claim: This is the first evidence that brain stimulation may promptly attenuate implicit defensive reactions during memory retrieval
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first evidence that brain stimulation may promptly attenuate implicit defensive reactions during memory retrieval.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature and current experimental findings

claim: The aPFC group displayed overall attenuated responses to tones relative to the sham condition
source: In the test session, we also analyzed threat generalization to the NSs through a 2 × 3 mixed ANOVA, which showed a significant main effect of group (F(1,58) = 5.310, p=0.025, ηp2 = 0.084), a nonsignificant main effect of tone (F(2,116) = 0.690, p=0.504, ηp2 = 0.012), and a nonsignificant group × tone interaction (F(2,116) = 1.301, p=0.276, ηp2 = 0.022), revealing that the aPFC group displayed overall attenuated responses to tones relative to the sham condition (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (ANOVA, p=0.025 for group effect)

claim: The rTMS did not cause an overall inhibition of electrodermal reactivity
source: No significant differences emerged between conditions (t(58) = 0.334, p=0.739, ηp2 = 0.002), indicating that the rTMS did not cause an overall inhibition of electrodermal reactivity (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing no difference in SCRs to US2 between groups (t-test, p=0.739)

claim: Participants of the aPFC group persisted in displaying weaker SCRs than those observed in the sham group during the follow-up session
source: Simple main effects analysis revealed that participants of the aPFC group persisted in displaying weaker SCRs than those observed in the sham group (p=0.006; Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.006, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The aPFC group persisted in showing a decrease of defensive reactions to the CS from conditioning to follow-up
source: Moreover, the aPFC group persisted in showing a decrease of defensive reactions to the CS from conditioning to follow-up (p<0.001; Bonferroni corrected)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The sham group did not display significantly different SCRs in the conditioning and follow-up phases
source: while the sham group did not display significantly different SCRs in the two phases (p=0.787; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.787, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The findings support an enduring effect of the aPFC-rTMS in attenuating the long-term implicit defensive responses to the learned threat-predictive cue, even with the re-exposition to the environment where threat learning had occurred
source: These findings support an enduring effect of the aPFC-rTMS in attenuating the long-term implicit defensive responses to the learned threat-predictive cue, even with the re-exposition to the environment where threat learning had occurred.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing persistent effects during follow-up in the original context

claim: Reactions to the female scream sample (US2) did not differ between groups during the follow-up session
source: We next analyzed the autonomous response patterns to the female scream sample (unconditioned stimulus 2 [US2]) and again we found that reactions did not differ between groups (t(58) = 0.057, p=0.955, ηp2 < 0.001) (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.955)

claim: The persistent effect was expressed notwithstanding an unaffected electrodermal overall reactivity
source: Thus, the persistent effect was expressed notwithstanding an unaffected electrodermal overall reactivity.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of difference in US2 responses between groups

claim: The ctrl discomfort group showed no significantly different CS-evoked SCR levels to those of the sham group during the test session
source: This group showed no significantly different CS-evoked SCR levels to those of the sham group during the test session as well as during the follow-up session (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The ctrl discomfort group showed no significantly different CS-evoked SCR levels to those of the sham group during the follow-up session
source: This group showed no significantly different CS-evoked SCR levels to those of the sham group during the test session as well as during the follow-up session (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The discomfort experienced during the rTMS procedure did not contribute to the reduction of electrodermal responses observed in the aPFC-stimulated group
source: Thus, the discomfort experienced during the rTMS procedure did not contribute to the reduction of electrodermal responses observed in the aPFC-stimulated group.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of effect in the ctrl discomfort group

claim: Both aPFC-E and sham-E groups successfully identified the CS amongst the NSs with an accuracy level above the 50% chance level
source: Both groups reported nonsignificantly different post-conditioning US ratings (t(40) = 0.339, p=0.737, ηp2 = 0.003) and successfully identified the CS amongst the NSs with an accuracy level above the 50% chance level (aPFC-E: t(20) = 9.226, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.810; sham-E: t(20) = 14.240, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.910).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (one-sample t-tests, p<0.001 for both groups)

claim: There were no differences in the explicit recognition accuracy between aPFC-E and sham-E groups
source: A between-groups comparison (t(40) = 1.114, p=0.272, ηp2 = 0.030) showed no differences in the explicit recognition accuracy (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.272)

claim: The two groups (aPFC-E and sham-E) were not differently confident when making their explicit recognition choices
source: The two groups were not differently confident when making their choices (t(40) = 0.842, p=0.405, ηp2 = 0.017) (Figure 3B), thereby supporting the lack of rTMS-related effects.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.405)

claim: The perceptual discrimination test yielded no significant between-groups differences in accuracy
source: The perceptual discrimination test yielded no significant between-groups differences in accuracy (t(40) = 1.362, p=0.181, ηp2 = 0.044) as well as confidence levels (t(40) = 0.917, p=0.365, ηp2 = 0.021).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.181)

claim: The perceptual discrimination test yielded no significant between-groups differences in confidence levels
source: The perceptual discrimination test yielded no significant between-groups differences in accuracy (t(40) = 1.362, p=0.181, ηp2 = 0.044) as well as confidence levels (t(40) = 0.917, p=0.365, ηp2 = 0.021).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.365)

claim: Both aPFC-E and sham-E groups discriminated the CS from the NSs with high precision
source: Indeed, both groups discriminated the CS from the NSs with high precision (aPFC-E: 0.980 ± 0.015 SEM; sham-E: 1.000 ± 0.000 SEM) and with no different confidence levels (aPFC-E: 9.409 ± 0.153 SEM; sham-E: 9.586 ± 0.117 SEM), thereby showing no rTMS effects on sensory abilities.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing high discrimination accuracy in both groups

claim: The pre-retrieval rTMS procedure over the aPFC did not affect the explicit recognition of a learned threat
source: These data suggest that the pre-retrieval rTMS procedure over the aPFC did not affect the explicit recognition nor the perceptual discrimination of a learned threat.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of differences between aPFC-E and sham-E groups in explicit recognition tasks

claim: The pre-retrieval rTMS procedure over the aPFC did not affect the perceptual discrimination of a learned threat
source: These data suggest that the pre-retrieval rTMS procedure over the aPFC did not affect the explicit recognition nor the perceptual discrimination of a learned threat.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of differences between aPFC-E and sham-E groups in perceptual discrimination tasks

claim: During the follow-up session, explicit recognition patterns demonstrated an over-chance accuracy level for each group (aPFC-E and sham-E)
source: During the follow-up session, explicit recognition patterns demonstrated an over-chance accuracy level for each group (aPFC-E: t(20) = 13.780, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.905; sham-E: t(20) = 7.162, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.720).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (one-sample t-tests, p<0.001 for both groups)

claim: There were no between-group differences in explicit recognition accuracy during the follow-up session
source: Again, here there were no between-group differences (t(40) = 1.024, p=0.312, ηp2 = 0.026) since both groups achieved a high recognition accuracy (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.312)

claim: Groups did not report different confidence levels during the follow-up explicit recognition test
source: Groups did also not report different confidence levels (t(40) = 0.084, p=0.934, ηp2 < 0.001) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.934)

claim: There were no significant between-group differences in the perceptual discrimination during the follow-up session
source: As in the case of the previous session, we did not observe significant between-group differences in the perceptual discrimination (t(40) = 1.000, p=0.323, ηp2 = 0.024) and the respective confidence ratings (t(40) = 0.149, p=0.882, ηp2 < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.323)

claim: There were no significant between-group differences in the perceptual discrimination confidence ratings during the follow-up session
source: As in the case of the previous session, we did not observe significant between-group differences in the perceptual discrimination (t(40) = 1.000, p=0.323, ηp2 = 0.024) and the respective confidence ratings (t(40) = 0.149, p=0.882, ηp2 < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (t-test, p=0.882)

claim: During the test, the aPFC group exhibited weaker defensive responses than the OC group
source: CS-related SCRs did not differ between groups during conditioning (p=0.798; Bonferroni corrected) but, during the test, the aPFC group exhibited weaker defensive responses than the OC group (p=0.019; Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.019, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The aPFC group's implicit reactions to the CS diminished from conditioning to test
source: Unlike the aPFC group, whose implicit reactions to the CS diminished from conditioning to test (p=0.014; Bonferroni corrected), the OC group's responses did not differ in the two phases (p=0.600; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.014, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The OC group's responses did not differ between conditioning and test phases
source: Unlike the aPFC group, whose implicit reactions to the CS diminished from conditioning to test (p=0.014; Bonferroni corrected), the OC group's responses did not differ in the two phases (p=0.600; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.600, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The CS triggered weaker reactions in the aPFC group compared to the OC group
source: While the CS triggered weaker reactions in the aPFC group (p=0.019; Bonferroni corrected), both the NS1 (p=0.203; Bonferroni corrected) and the NS2 (p=0.323; Bonferroni corrected) elicited nonsignificantly different responses in the two conditions.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.019, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: In the OC group, the NS2 evoked lower SCRs than the CS
source: In the case of the OC group, implicit reactions were not different for the CS and the NS1 (p=0.876; Bonferroni corrected) but the NS2 evoked lower SCRs than the CS (p<0.001; Bonferroni corrected) and the NS1 (p=0.041; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: In the OC group, the NS2 evoked lower SCRs than the NS1
source: In the case of the OC group, implicit reactions were not different for the CS and the NS1 (p=0.876; Bonferroni corrected) but the NS2 evoked lower SCRs than the CS (p<0.001; Bonferroni corrected) and the NS1 (p=0.041; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.041, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The aPFC group continued to react more dimly to the CS compared to the OC group during the follow-up session
source: The aPFC group continued to react more dimly to the CS compared to the OC group (p=0.026; Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.026, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: Both the aPFC and the OC groups showed decreased responses relative to conditioning during the follow-up session
source: Both the aPFC (p<0.001; Bonferroni corrected) and the OC (p=0.022; Bonferroni corrected) groups showed decreased responses relative to conditioning (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001 and p=0.022, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: During the test phase, the group stimulated over the aPFC displayed lower reactions than the dlPFC group
source: CS-evoked SCRs did not differ between the two groups during conditioning (p=0.647; Bonferroni corrected) while during the test we found weaker defensive responses in the aPFC group relative to the dlPFC group (p=0.009; Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.009, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The aPFC group's implicit reactions to the CS were diminished from conditioning to test
source: At odds with the aPFC group whose implicit reactions to the CS were diminished from conditioning to test (p=0.013; Bonferroni corrected), the dlPFC group increasingly responded during the test relative to conditioning (p=0.042; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.013, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The dlPFC group increasingly responded during the test relative to conditioning
source: At odds with the aPFC group whose implicit reactions to the CS were diminished from conditioning to test (p=0.013; Bonferroni corrected), the dlPFC group increasingly responded during the test relative to conditioning (p=0.042; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.042, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The incremental trend in the dlPFC group is in line with a previous study that delivered a 1 Hz-rTMS protocol over the left dlPFC
source: This incremental trend is in line with a previous study that delivered a 1 Hz-rTMS protocol over the left dlPFC (Borgomaneri et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Borgomaneri et al., 2020

claim: In the dlPFC group, the NS2 evoked lower SCRs than the CS
source: Fear tuning analysis of the dlPFC group's implicit reactions revealed no different SCR amplitudes elicited by the CS and the NS1 (p=0.158; Bonferroni corrected) and by the NSs (p=0.721; Bonferroni corrected), but the NS2 evoked lower SCRs than the CS (p=0.014; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.014, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The aPFC group persisted in more dimly reacting to the CS with respect to the dlPFC group during the follow-up session
source: The different pattern toward the learned threatening cue was replicated during the follow-up session (2 × 2 mixed ANOVA; main effect of group: F(1,58) = 3.751, p=0.058, ηp2 = 0.061; main effect of phase: F(1,58) = 3.114, p=0.083, ηp2 = 0.051; group × phase interaction: F(1,58) = 15.248, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.208) since the aPFC group persisted in more dimly reacting to the CS with respect to the dlPFC group (p=0.001; Bonferroni corrected)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.001, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The aPFC group endured in displaying attenuated responses relative to conditioning during the follow-up session
source: and the aPFC group endured in displaying attenuated responses relative to conditioning (p<0.001; Bonferroni corrected) while the dlPFC group did not (p=0.136; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p<0.001, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: The dlPFC group did not display attenuated responses relative to conditioning during the follow-up session
source: and the aPFC group endured in displaying attenuated responses relative to conditioning (p<0.001; Bonferroni corrected) while the dlPFC group did not (p=0.136; Bonferroni corrected) (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (p=0.136, Bonferroni corrected)

claim: rTMS over the left dorsolateral PFC did not diminish implicit defensive reactions in the absence of an extinction paradigm
source: These findings demonstrated that rTMS over the left dorsolateral PFC did not diminish implicit defensive reactions in the absence of an extinction paradigm, as in other previous studies (Guhn et al., 2014; Raij et al., 2018; Borgomaneri et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and comparison with previous studies

claim: rTMS targeting the aPFC proved to be effective in diminishing implicit defensive reactions in the absence of an extinction paradigm
source: Meanwhile, rTMS targeting the aPFC proved to be effective in achieving this outcome.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing reduced responses in aPFC group

claim: Most rTMS studies targeting the prefrontal cortex have been conducted to enhance fear extinction processes
source: So far, most rTMS studies targeting the prefrontal cortex have been conducted to enhance fear extinction processes.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: 10 Hz-rTMS over the mPFC observed enhancement of extinction learning
source: A study (Guhn et al., 2014) administering one session of 10 Hz-rTMS over the mPFC observed enhancement of extinction learning.
evidence: Supported by citation to Guhn et al., 2014

claim: Increased mPFC activity was revealed in the stimulated group relative to the sham group by fNIRS findings
source: These behavioral results were mirrored by the functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) findings, which revealed increased mPFC activity in the stimulated group relative to the sham group (Guhn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guhn et al., 2014

claim: Brief 20 Hz-rTMS trains over the left posterior PFC during extinction learning found a reduction of defensive responses during extinction recall
source: Subsequently, Raij et al., 2018 delivered brief 20 Hz-rTMS trains over the left posterior PFC ‒ a region that showed robust functional connectivity with the vmPFC‒ during extinction learning and found a reduction of defensive responses during extinction recall.
evidence: Supported by citation to Raij et al., 2018

claim: The current study tested rTMS effects over the medial aPFC (medial BA 10)
source: Our study differs from the previous ones because we tested rTMS effects over the medial aPFC (medial BA 10), and we did not include extinction training before retrieval.
evidence: Based on description of experimental methods

claim: The current study did not include extinction training before retrieval
source: Our study differs from the previous ones because we tested rTMS effects over the medial aPFC (medial BA 10), and we did not include extinction training before retrieval.
evidence: Based on description of experimental methods

claim: A significant decrease in defensive reactions was observed shortly after rTMS
source: We observed a significant decrease in defensive reactions shortly after rTMS, and this effect was maintained until the follow-up session.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing reduced SCRs in aPFC group during test session

claim: The effect of rTMS was maintained until the follow-up session
source: We observed a significant decrease in defensive reactions shortly after rTMS, and this effect was maintained until the follow-up session.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing persistent reduced SCRs in aPFC group during follow-up session

claim: The study identified a previously unexplored prefrontal region, the modulation of which can efficiently and durably inhibit implicit reactions to learned threats
source: Thus, we identified a previously unexplored prefrontal region, the modulation of which can efficiently and durably inhibit implicit reactions to learned threats.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings showing persistent effects of aPFC stimulation

claim: The dampening effects may be due to the fact that rTMS over the aPFC have directly modulated the defensive responses activated by the implicit threat memory trace
source: These dampening effects may be due to the fact that rTMS over the aPFC have directly modulated the defensive responses activated by the implicit threat memory trace.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying observed effects

claim: The rTMS procedure over the aPFC may have inhibited the recall of the CS-US association, preventing the defensive responses from being activated by the CS
source: Alternatively, the rTMS procedure over the aPFC may have inhibited the recall of the CS-US association, preventing the defensive responses from being activated by the CS.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying observed effects

claim: This possibility would be in line with a large body of literature on humans which demonstrates the importance of the medial PFC for value-based processing
source: This possibility would be in line with a large body of literature on humans (see Hiser and Koenigs, 2018), which demonstrates the importance of the medial PFC for value-based processing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hiser and Koenigs, 2018

claim: The lack of between-group differences in the autonomic responses to the US2 suggests that the observed effect may be memory-related and not due to a general dampening of autonomic reactivity
source: However, the lack of between-group differences in the autonomic responses to the US2 seems to suggest that the observed effect may be memory-related and not due to a general dampening of autonomic reactivity.
evidence: Based on inference from the lack of difference in US2 responses between groups

claim: Defensive responses toward the NSs were decreased following the stimulation of the left occipital cortex
source: Interestingly, defensive responses toward the NSs were decreased following the stimulation of the left occipital cortex (OC group, BA18/19).
evidence: Based on experimental data from the OC group

claim: Anatomical and functional reciprocal projections between the medial BA10 and visual association cortices have been traced via the fronto-occipital fasciculus of the human brain
source: This effect might be explained by the fact that anatomical and functional reciprocal projections between the medial BA10 and visual association cortices (including BA17/18/19) have been traced via the fronto-occipital fasciculus (FOF) of the human brain (Catani et al., 2012; Orr et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; but see Peng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Catani et al., 2012; Orr et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2016; Peng et al., 2018

claim: The inhibition of SCR responses induced by rTMS during the mnemonic retention test could have persistently reduced such conditioned responses even at a distance from the treatment
source: Firstly, the inhibition of SCR responses induced by rTMS during the mnemonic retention test could have persistently reduced such conditioned responses even at a distance from the treatment.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying persistent effects

claim: The inhibition of responses during the test might have boosted the extinction of these responses, contributing to keeping them low over time
source: Moreover, the inhibition of these responses during the test might have boosted the extinction of these responses, contributing to keeping them low over time.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying persistent effects

claim: Under certain circumstances such as a simple passage of time or a change in surrounding context, extinguished reactions triggered by the CS may reoccur, giving rise to the phenomenon known as return of fear
source: On this possibility, it should be pointed out that one core knowledge about extinction is that under certain circumstances ‒ such as a simple passage of time (i.e., spontaneous recovery) or a change in surrounding context (i.e., renewal) ‒ extinguished reactions triggered by the CS may reoccur, giving rise to the phenomenon known as return of fear (Vervliet et al., 2013; Pavlov, 1927; Rachman, 1966).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vervliet et al., 2013; Pavlov, 1927; Rachman, 1966

claim: The aPFC-rTMS protocol long-term reduced threat memory expression in a different context as well as in the context in which the threatening experience had occurred, thus preventing the return of fear
source: These data demonstrated that the aPFC-rTMS protocol long-term reduced threat memory expression in a different context as well as in the context in which the threatening experience had occurred, thus preventing the return of fear.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing persistent effects across contexts

claim: The rTMS applied immediately before the mnemonic retention test may have interfered with the reconsolidation process, resulting in a persistent impairment in the retention of this mnemonic trace
source: Finally, we cannot exclude that the rTMS applied immediately before the mnemonic retention test interfered with the reconsolidation process that is known to occur after this test (Su et al., 2022), resulting in a persistent impairment in the retention of this mnemonic trace.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying persistent effects, with citation to Su et al., 2022

claim: High-frequency rTMS protocols are conventionally considered excitatory of proximal brain activity
source: To potentiate the neural activity of the PFC, both the aforementioned studies (Guhn et al., 2014; Raij et al., 2018) adopted high-frequency rTMS protocols, which are conventionally considered excitatory of proximal brain activity (Pascual-Leone et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guhn et al., 2014; Raij et al., 2018; Pascual-Leone et al., 1998

claim: Low-frequency rTMS protocols are conventionally considered inhibitory
source: In our study, we adopted a low-frequency rTMS protocol, which is conventionally considered inhibitory (Pascual-Leone et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pascual-Leone et al., 1998

claim: Recent evidence challenged the common frequency-dependent rule for rTMS effects
source: Recent evidence, however, challenged this common frequency-dependent rule (Luber and Deng, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luber and Deng, 2016

claim: 1 Hz-rTMS protocols may induce downstream distal effects and enhance functional connectivity amongst the brain regions located underneath the coil and remote brain areas of the stimulated neural network
source: Resting-state functional MRI studies demonstrated that 1 Hz-rTMS protocols may also induce downstream distal effects and enhance functional connectivity amongst the brain regions located underneath the coil and remote brain areas of the stimulated neural network (Beynel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beynel et al., 2020

claim: 1 Hz-rTMS procedures delivered over the PFC may paradoxically increase regional cerebral blood flow
source: Additionally, some studies (Eisenegger et al., 2008; Nahas et al., 2001) reported that 1 Hz-rTMS procedures delivered over the PFC may paradoxically increase regional cerebral blood flow.
evidence: Supported by citations to Eisenegger et al., 2008; Nahas et al., 2001

claim: The dorsolateral PFC is assumed to be critically involved in threat learning
source: The dorsolateral PFC is another prefrontal region that is assumed to be critically involved in threat learning (Dunsmoor et al., 2007; Dunsmoor et al., 2008) and the downregulation of the cortico-meso-limbic network (Vicario et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dunsmoor et al., 2007; Dunsmoor et al., 2008; Vicario et al., 2019

claim: 1 Hz-rTMS over the dlPFC after memory reactivation was used to disrupt threat-memory reconsolidation
source: One investigation (Borgomaneri et al., 2020) probed the effects of a 1 Hz-rTMS over the dlPFC after memory reactivation to disrupt threat-memory reconsolidation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Borgomaneri et al., 2020

claim: Stimulated groups in the Borgomaneri et al. study failed to discriminate between threatening and safe stimuli, with an increase in autonomic responses to safe stimuli
source: Stimulated groups failed to discriminate between threatening and safe stimuli, with an increase in autonomic responses to these last ones.
evidence: Supported by citation to Borgomaneri et al., 2020

claim: Continuous theta-burst stimulation over the right dlPFC during the reconsolidation window successfully decreased the defensive responses for threat memories
source: A more recent study (Su et al., 2022) adopted the continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) over the right dlPFC during the reconsolidation window and successfully decreased the defensive responses for threat memories.
evidence: Supported by citation to Su et al., 2022

claim: An immediate and long-term reduction of defensive responses to the CS was found only in subjects that were stimulated over the aPFC
source: In our study, we found an immediate and long-term reduction of defensive responses to the CS only in subjects that were stimulated over the aPFC, while reactions to the NSs were decreased in both conditions.
evidence: Based on experimental data comparing aPFC and dlPFC groups

claim: Targeting the aPFC might represent a more promising approach for therapeutic applications
source: This evidence suggests that targeting the aPFC might represent a more promising approach for therapeutic applications.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing superior effects of aPFC stimulation

claim: The lack of downregulation of CS-evoked reactions in the dlPFC group might be due to the fact that the study did not adopt an extinction paradigm
source: The lack of any downregulation of CS-evoked reactions that we found in the dlPFC group, at odds with previous studies targeting the same cortical area (Borgomaneri et al., 2020; Su et al., 2022), might be due either to the fact that we did not adopt an extinction paradigm or to the different brain stimulation approach (rTMS vs. cTBS).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of differences from previous studies

claim: The lack of downregulation of CS-evoked reactions in the dlPFC group might be due to the different brain stimulation approach (rTMS vs. cTBS)
source: The lack of any downregulation of CS-evoked reactions that we found in the dlPFC group, at odds with previous studies targeting the same cortical area (Borgomaneri et al., 2020; Su et al., 2022), might be due either to the fact that we did not adopt an extinction paradigm or to the different brain stimulation approach (rTMS vs. cTBS).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of differences from previous studies

claim: Fear memories are formed and retrieved by an intricate neural network encompassing the amygdala, the cerebellum, and sensory cortices
source: Fear memories are formed and retrieved by an intricate neural network encompassing the amygdala (Pape and Pare, 2010), the cerebellum (Sacchetti et al., 2002; Sacchetti et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2011), and sensory cortices (Sacco and Sacchetti, 2010; Grosso et al., 2015; Manassero et al., 2018; Cambiaghi et al., 2016a; Cambiaghi et al., 2016b; Concina et al., 2019; You et al., 2021; You et al., 2022; Ojala et al., 2022; Monfils, 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to relevant literature

claim: Previous evidence showed both structural connections between the aPFC and the amygdala
source: Indeed, previous evidence showed both structural connections between the aPFC and the amygdala (Bramson et al., 2020; Folloni et al., 2019; Peng et al., 2018) and a connectivity pathway of downstream modulation from the aPFC to the vmPFC (Fonzo et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bramson et al., 2020; Folloni et al., 2019; Peng et al., 2018

claim: A connectivity pathway of downstream modulation from the aPFC to the vmPFC exists
source: Indeed, previous evidence showed both structural connections between the aPFC and the amygdala (Bramson et al., 2020; Folloni et al., 2019; Peng et al., 2018) and a connectivity pathway of downstream modulation from the aPFC to the vmPFC (Fonzo et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fonzo et al., 2017b

claim: The aPFC-vmPFC projection is activated during fear regulation, possibly supporting the vmPFC in top-down modulating the amygdala
source: This projection is activated during fear regulation (Klumpers et al., 2010), possibly supporting the vmPFC in top-down modulating the amygdala (Motzkin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klumpers et al., 2010 and Motzkin et al., 2015

claim: Through the direct or indirect connections of the aPFC with these areas, the effects of focal manipulations of aPFC activity might reflect complex and dynamic changes in the overall neural network state
source: Through the direct or indirect connections of the aPFC with these areas, it might be that the effects of focal manipulations of aPFC activity reflect complex and dynamic changes in the overall neural network state and/or influence the activity of some of these areas.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying observed effects

claim: Previous studies enlightened the role of the medial BA10 and BA10‒posterior hippocampus functional connectivity in episodic memory retrieval
source: Although previous studies enlightened the role of the medial BA10 and BA10‒posterior hippocampus functional connectivity in episodic memory retrieval (see Faran, 2023), we did not detect any rTMS-driven effect on explicit recognition memory.
evidence: Supported by citation to Faran, 2023

claim: The observed divergence between autonomous and declarative patterns might have been due to a selective rTMS action upon the neural system supporting implicit threat processing
source: The observed divergence between autonomous and declarative patterns might have been due to a selective rTMS action upon the neural system supporting implicit threat processing, which has been widely dissociated from the neural system underlying explicit memory processes (Bechara et al., 1995; LaBar and Cabeza, 2006; Knight et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative interpretation with support from citations to Bechara et al., 1995; LaBar and Cabeza, 2006; Knight et al., 2009

claim: An rTMS procedure that shapes implicit overreactions to learned threats without affecting conscious knowledge of danger might represent a strategic advantage for therapeutic applications
source: Critically, an rTMS procedure that shapes implicit overreactions to learned threats without affecting conscious knowledge of danger might represent a strategic advantage for therapeutic applications.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings showing dissociation between implicit and explicit effects

claim: The findings may represent an advance by providing a potential strategy to deactivate emotional overreactions and prevent the return of fear
source: Since prevention of relapse is the main challenge for therapies dedicated to post-traumatic and anxiety disorders, our findings may represent an advance in this direction by providing a potential strategy to deactivate emotional overreactions and, most of all, to prevent the return of fear.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings showing persistent effects and prevention of renewal

claim: All participants were healthy volunteers with no history of psychiatric disorders, neurological illnesses, cardiovascular diseases, illegal drug use, musical training, or any other exclusion criteria for rTMS administration
source: All participants (n = 183) were healthy volunteers (mean age: 23.86 ± 2.90, 74 males and 109 females) with no history of psychiatric disorders, neurological illnesses, cardiovascular diseases, illegal drug use, musical training, or any other exclusion criteria for rTMS administration (Rossi et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on description of participant inclusion criteria

claim: Volunteers who showed a score >80 in the sum of the State + Trait anxiety subscales were not included in the sample
source: During the pre-experimental screening phase, each volunteer was also administered the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory Form Y (Spielberger et al., 1983; Pedrabissi and Santinello, 1989), and those who showed a score >80 in the sum of the two subscales (State + Trait anxiety) were not included in the sample (see Table 1 for all groups' mean State-Trait Anxiety Inventory scores).
evidence: Based on description of participant exclusion criteria

claim: 11 participants were discarded because of a complete absence of SCRs during the test session
source: We discarded 11 participants because of a complete absence of SCRs during the test session, leaving a total of 172 participants.
evidence: Based on description of data exclusion criteria

claim: A single-cue learning paradigm was adopted because it more ecologically reflects real-life traumatic experiences
source: We adopted a single-cue learning paradigm because it more ecologically reflects real-life traumatic experiences (Resnik and Paz, 2015; Wong and Lovibond, 2017; Grosso et al., 2018; Concina et al., 2018; Grosso et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Resnik and Paz, 2015; Wong and Lovibond, 2017; Grosso et al., 2018; Concina et al., 2018; Grosso et al., 2017

claim: Memory retention was tested in a different environment from that where the learning had occurred to avoid any contextual influence on retrieval
source: Memory retention was tested in a different environment from that where the learning had occurred (context B) to avoid any contextual influence on retrieval (Manassero et al., 2019; Ameli et al., 2001; Maren et al., 2013; Sacco and Sacchetti, 2010; Sacchetti et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manassero et al., 2019; Ameli et al., 2001; Maren et al., 2013; Sacco and Sacchetti, 2010; Sacchetti et al., 1999

claim: The context shift for the test session mirrors a real-life treatment setting, which unlikely takes place in the threatening location
source: Indeed, the context shift for this session mirrors a real-life treatment setting, which unlikely takes place in the threatening location.
evidence: Based on inference about ecological validity of experimental design

claim: Auditory frequencies of NSs were selected to obtain a slowly decaying gradient of defensive tunings
source: Auditory frequencies of NSs were selected to obtain a slowly decaying gradient of defensive tunings (Manassero et al., 2019; Onat and Büchel, 2015; Laufer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manassero et al., 2019; Onat and Büchel, 2015; Laufer et al., 2016

claim: The coil was positioned over the frontopolar midline electrode (Fpz) adopting the international 10‒20 EEG coordinate system to target the medial aPFC
source: To locate this brain region, which corresponds to the BA 10 (Hanlon et al., 2018), we positioned the coil over the frontopolar midline electrode (Fpz) adopting the international 10‒20 electroencephalogram (EEG) coordinate system (Jasper, 1958) since previous rTMS studies (Guhn et al., 2014; Herrmann et al., 2017; Karmann et al., 2016) ensured this placement reached the aPFC.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hanlon et al., 2018; Jasper, 1958; Guhn et al., 2014; Herrmann et al., 2017; Karmann et al., 2016

claim: All participants were blinded to their experimental condition (active or sham)
source: All participants were blinded to their experimental condition (i.e., active or sham) and were not informed about the potential cognitive or emotional effects of the stimulation.
evidence: Based on description of experimental blinding procedures

claim: Participants were not informed about the potential cognitive or emotional effects of the stimulation
source: All participants were blinded to their experimental condition (i.e., active or sham) and were not informed about the potential cognitive or emotional effects of the stimulation.
evidence: Based on description of experimental blinding procedures

claim: A 2AFC design was preferred over a new-old paradigm because it improves recognition performance and discourages response biases
source: As in our previous works (Manassero et al., 2019; Manassero et al., 2022), a 2AFC design was preferred over a new-old paradigm, which involves one single stimulus on each trial, and the subject judges whether the stimulus has been previously encoded (old), or whether it is new. Our choice was motivated by the evidence that a 2AFC task improves recognition performance and discourages response biases such as the familiarity-based decision bias, namely the heuristic to endorse novel cues as 'old' when their familiarity is high (Macmillan and Creelman, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manassero et al., 2019; Manassero et al., 2022; Macmillan and Creelman, 2004

claim: Event-related SCRs were used as an implicit index of defensive responses
source: Event-related SCRs were used as an implicit index of defensive responses.
evidence: Based on established methodology in psychophysiology

claim: Raw SCR values were scaled according to each participant's average unconditioned response by dividing each response by the mean US response during the conditioning phase
source: To account for inter-individual variability, these raw values were then scaled according to each participant's average unconditioned response by dividing each response by the mean US response during the conditioning phase (Schiller et al., 2010; Battaglia et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schiller et al., 2010; Battaglia et al., 2018

claim: Scaled SCR data were square-root transformed to normalize the distributions
source: Scaled SCR data were square-root transformed to normalize the distributions (Lykken and Venables, 1971).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lykken and Venables, 1971

claim: For the main statistics, the estimated sample size resulted in n = 30 per experimental group
source: We computed the appropriate sample size based on a power analysis performed through G*Power 3.1.9.2. For the main statistics, that is, mixed ANOVA (within–between interaction) with two groups and two measurements, with the following input parameters: α = 0.05, power (1-β) = 0.95, and a hypothesized effect size (f) = 0.25, the estimated sample size resulted in n = 30 per experimental group.
evidence: Based on power analysis calculation
